New physics in the form vector and axial-vector couplings is already severely constrained by the data on B --> (K,K*) mu+ mu-. # Constraints on New Physics Contributions to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ from B_s–B̄_s Mixing

This letter examines how recent measurements of B_s–B̄_s mixing constrain possible new physics contributions to the rare decay B_s → μ⁺μ⁻. As one of the most sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model, this leptonic decay has attracted considerable theoretical and experimental attention. Understanding the extent to which new physics can modify its branching ratio requires a careful analysis of the complementary experimental information available from related processes.

New physics scenarios involving vector and axial-vector couplings are already severely restricted by existing data. In particular, measurements of the semileptonic decays B → (K, K*) μ⁺μ⁻ place stringent limits on these types of interactions. Because these decays are governed by the same underlying quark-level transitions, any large new physics contributions of the vector or axial-vector type would produce observable deviations in their rates and distributions. The consistency of current data with Standard Model predictions therefore leaves little room for such contributions to significantly enhance B_s → μ⁺μ⁻.

The remaining possibility lies in scalar and pseudoscalar interactions. Here, the recent B_s–B̄_s mixing data play a decisive role. When combined with well-established constraints from K⁰–K̄⁰ mixing and the measured K_L → μ⁺μ⁻ decay rate, these data strongly restrict the scalar-pseudoscalar contribution to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻. Together, these observables form a network of correlated constraints that bound the size of the relevant new physics operators.

Taken as a whole, these combined constraints lead to a clear and important conclusion: new physics can at most produce a factor of two increase in the branching ratio of B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ relative to the Standard Model expectation. This result establishes a robust upper limit on the possible enhancement of this decay, providing a valuable benchmark for interpreting present and future experimental measurements.

# Constraints on New Physics Contributions to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ from Meson Mixing and Rare Decay Data

## Introduction

The rare decay B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ has long been recognized as a sensitive probe of physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). Within the SM, this decay proceeds through loop-level electroweak processes and is further suppressed by helicity considerations, resulting in a small branching ratio of order 10⁻⁹. This strong suppression makes the channel particularly attractive for new physics searches, as even modest additional contributions—especially those mediated by scalar or pseudoscalar operators that evade the helicity suppression—could substantially enhance the observed rate. Consequently, a large enhancement of the B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ branching ratio has often been considered a potential smoking gun for new physics in the flavor sector.

However, the freedom to introduce such new contributions is not unbounded. The same scalar and pseudoscalar couplings that could enhance B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ generally contribute to other observable processes, most notably to neutral meson mixing. In this letter, we systematically examine how recent measurements of B_s–B̄_s mixing, taken together with well-established constraints from K⁰–K̄⁰ mixing and the rare decay K_L → μ⁺μ⁻, restrict the allowed size of new physics effects in B_s → μ⁺μ⁻.

## Theoretical Framework

New physics contributions involving scalar-pseudoscalar couplings can be parametrized through an effective Lagrangian containing four-fermion operators of the form (b̄Γs)(μ̄Γ′μ), where Γ and Γ′ denote scalar or pseudoscalar Dirac structures. Crucially, these same couplings, when combined with the analogous quark-bilinear operators (b̄Γs)(b̄Γ′s), generate contributions to B_s–B̄_s mixing. The correlation between the leptonic decay amplitude and the mixing amplitude arises naturally in a broad class of models where the new physics couples to both quark and lepton currents through a common mediator.

By exploiting this correlation, one can translate the experimental bounds on the B_s mass difference, ΔM_s, into limits on the product of couplings responsible for the leptonic decay. The recent precise determination of ΔM_s provides a particularly powerful constraint, since any large scalar-pseudoscalar contribution to the decay would be accompanied by a corresponding shift in the mixing observable that is now tightly measured.

## Complementary Constraints

To close potential loopholes and to bound couplings involving the down and strange quark sectors, we incorporate two additional sources of experimental information. First, K⁰–K̄⁰ mixing constrains the scalar-pseudoscalar operators built from down-type quark currents, complementing the information obtained from the B_s system. Second, the measured branching ratio of K_L → μ⁺μ⁻ directly bounds the leptonic coupling structure in a manner analogous to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻, but in the kaon sector. Taken together, these observables span a range of quark flavor combinations and lepton couplings, allowing a comprehensive assessment of the allowed parameter space.

## Results and Conclusions

Combining all available constraints, we find that the room for new physics enhancement of the B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ branching ratio is considerably more limited than one might naively expect. Specifically, our analysis demonstrates that new physics contributions, when consistent with the measured B_s–B̄_s mixing, K⁰–K̄⁰ mixing, and K_L → μ⁺μ⁻ data, can increase the B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ branching ratio by at most a factor of 2 relative to the SM prediction.

This result has important implications for the interpretation of current and future measurements. It indicates that the observation of a large deviation from the SM value in this decay channel is strongly disfavored once existing flavor constraints are taken into account. Rather than serving as a channel where order-of-magnitude enhancements might be expected, B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ appears to be tightly bounded to remain close to its SM value. Any measured branching ratio significantly exceeding twice the SM prediction would therefore signal either a breakdown of the correlations assumed here or the presence of new physics operating through mechanisms not captured by simple scalar-pseudoscalar couplings.

These findings underscore the value of a global approach to flavor physics, in which correlations among different observables provide powerful, model-independent constraints on the scope for new phenomena in individual decay channels.
outputs.L5:
# The New Standard Is Here

Change has a way of sneaking up on us. One day we're comfortable with how things have always been done, and the next, something new arrives that makes us wonder how we ever managed before. This is the moment we find ourselves in now—a shift from the old ways toward something better, something more refined.

## Embracing What's New

The word "new" carries a special kind of energy. It promises improvement, innovation, and the excitement of possibility. But being new isn't enough on its own. Plenty of new ideas come and go without leaving a mark. What separates a passing trend from a lasting transformation is quality and purpose.

When something new truly earns its place, it doesn't just add to the noise—it clarifies it. It solves problems we didn't even realize we had and opens doors we didn't know existed.

## The Standard Has Changed

For too long, we accepted "good enough" as the benchmark. We tolerated inefficiency, complexity, and compromise because we had no reason to expect more. But standards are not fixed. They rise when someone decides to raise them.

A new standard means redefining expectations. It means refusing to settle for what came before and committing to something more thoughtful, more effective, and more aligned with what people actually need.

## Here and Now

The most important word might be the simplest: *here*. Not coming soon. Not on the horizon. Here—available, ready, and waiting to be embraced.

The future doesn't announce itself with fanfare. It arrives quietly, in the choices we make today. And right now, the choice is clear: step forward into what's new, accept the higher standard, and recognize that the moment has arrived.

The new standard is here. The only question is whether you're ready to meet it.

# Abstract

We investigate the correlation between $B_s$–$\bar{B}_s$ mixing and the rare leptonic decay $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ within a broad class of new physics scenarios. Both observables are sensitive to flavor-changing neutral currents involving the $b \to s$ transition, making their interplay a powerful probe of physics beyond the Standard Model. Working in an effective field theory framework, we demonstrate that the measured mass difference $\Delta M_s$, in agreement with Standard Model predictions at the few-percent level, imposes stringent constraints on the Wilson coefficients that also govern the $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ amplitude. In particular, we show that in models featuring $Z'$ bosons or scalar-mediated tree-level contributions, the enhancement of the branching ratio $\mathcal{B}(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)$ is bounded by the requirement of consistency with $\Delta M_s$. We derive model-independent relations connecting the allowed deviation of $\mathcal{B}(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)$ from its Standard Model value to the shift in the mixing observable, and we quantify the resulting restrictions on the relevant coupling structures. Our analysis indicates that current data leave only limited room for new physics in $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, with the surviving parameter space to be further tested by upcoming measurements at the LHCb and Belle II experiments. These results underscore the complementarity of mixing and rare-decay observables in the global effort to constrain the flavor sector of new physics.

# Constraints on Scalar and Pseudoscalar New Physics Contributions to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻

## Introduction

The rare leptonic decay $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ provides one of the most sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model (SM), owing to its strong helicity suppression and the absence of tree-level flavor-changing neutral currents. Within the SM, this decay proceeds through electroweak loop diagrams and is theoretically clean, yielding a precise prediction for the branching ratio, $\mathcal{B}(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm SM} = (3.66 \pm 0.14) \times 10^{-9}$. New physics contributions mediated by scalar and pseudoscalar operators are particularly interesting, as they can lift the helicity suppression and induce sizable deviations from the SM expectation. However, such operators cannot be considered in isolation: the same underlying flavor-violating dynamics that modifies $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ generically feeds into meson mixing observables and correlated leptonic decays. In this work, we perform a systematic analysis of scalar and pseudoscalar new physics contributions to $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, incorporating the constraints imposed by $B_s$–$\bar{B}_s$ mixing, neutral kaon mixing, and the decay $K_L \to \mu^+\mu^-$. By confronting these complementary datasets simultaneously, we delineate the viable parameter space and demonstrate that the interplay of mixing observables with leptonic decay rates yields significantly tighter bounds than any single measurement in isolation, thereby sharpening the sensitivity to a broad class of extended scalar sectors.

---

For an actual publication, you should verify all numerical inputs against current experimental and theoretical references (e.g., HFLAV, PDG, and recent lattice determinations), and adjust the framing to match your specific model assumptions and results.*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Correlation Between B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ and B_s Mixing

The result you're referring to is a well-known model-independent bound that emerges when new physics contributions to B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ are correlated with B_s–B̄_s mixing constraints. Let me summarize the key argument.

## The Core Idea

The bound applies specifically to scenarios where new physics enters through **scalar and pseudoscalar operators** (the operators most capable of enhancing B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ beyond the SM). The connection arises because:

1. B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ is helicity-suppressed in the SM, making it especially sensitive to (pseudo)scalar contributions
2. The same underlying Higgs-mediated or new scalar interactions that generate these operators can also contribute to ΔM_s (the mass difference in B_s mixing)

## The Argument (Following Bobeth, Buras, et al.)

In models with tree-level scalar exchange (e.g., extended Higgs sectors, MSSM at large tan β), the effective couplings that generate the (pseudo)scalar operators for the leptonic decay simultaneously produce a **double-scalar-insertion** contribution to the mixing amplitude.

The crucial point is that the mixing observable ΔM_s constrains the **product of scalar couplings squared**, while B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ depends on the same combination. When you impose that new physics not spoil the (well-measured) agreement of ΔM_s with the SM prediction, the allowed enhancement of the branching ratio becomes bounded.

## The Result

Under these correlated constraints, the maximal enhancement is approximately

$$
\frac{\mathcal{B}(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)}{\mathcal{B}(B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-)_{\rm SM}} \lesssim 2
$$

i.e., new physics can **at most roughly double** the SM branching ratio.

## Important Caveats to State in Your Paper

- The bound is **not fully model-independent**: it relies on the assumption that the dominant new-physics effect comes through the specific scalar/pseudoscalar structure and that the same couplings dominate mixing.
- It can be **evaded** if:
  - Additional fields contribute to mixing with opposite sign (cancellations)
  - Vector/axial-vector operators (C₁₀-type) dominate instead
  - There are multiple mediators with tuned couplings
- The precise numerical factor depends on the input parameters (decay constant f_{B_s}, bag parameters, CKM elements) and the assumed correlation.

## References to Cite

The canonical references are likely:
- **A.J. Buras**, "Relations between ΔM_{s,d} and B_{s,d} → μ⁺μ⁻ in models with minimal flavour violation" (Phys. Lett. B **566** (2003) 115)
- **Bobeth, Ewerth, Krüger, Urban** — earlier work on scalar contributions in the MSSM

---

Would you like me to help with the explicit formulas relating the Wilson coefficients to both observables, or verify the numerical factor for a specific model (e.g., MFV, 2HDM, MSSM)? I'd also recommend double-checking the exact statement against the original papers, since the factor-of-2 result depends on the specific assumptions being invoked.

# Abstract

We present a comprehensive analysis constraining new physics contributions to the rare decay B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ within a model-independent effective Hamiltonian framework. Working with the full set of dimension-six operators, we systematically bound the vector, axial-vector, scalar, and pseudoscalar Wilson coefficients using currently available experimental data. Our fit combines the measured B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ branching ratio with complementary observables from the b → s sector, including B → K^(*)μ⁺μ⁻ differential rates and angular distributions, as well as leptonic and semileptonic K meson decays that provide orthogonal constraints on the scalar and pseudoscalar sectors.

We find that the axial-vector coupling remains tightly constrained by the branching ratio alone, while scalar and pseudoscalar contributions—to which B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ is uniquely sensitive owing to the absence of helicity suppression—are bounded most stringently when B and K observables are combined. The correlated limits reduce allowed parameter space by up to an order of magnitude relative to single-observable fits, disfavoring several new physics scenarios with enhanced (pseudo)scalar interactions. We quantify the interplay between these operator classes and discuss the projected impact of improved measurements from LHCb and Belle II. Our results establish B_s → μ⁺μ⁻ as a robust probe of physics beyond the Standard Model when interpreted alongside the broader landscape of flavor observables.

---

*Keywords:* rare B decays, effective field theory, Wilson coefficients, lepton flavor, new physics constraints
